blocks.x: So you were talking about when you joined Louis Armstrong.
Yeah, Louis came back. By the time Louis came back I had been studying on the Roy and Dutre. First one, first one I could catch. That was it.
Wait a minute. Okay, it's going now. Can you tell about when you joined Louis?

When I joined Louis, yeah. Louis came back. He was on his way to California to play at Sebastons. Which later became famous and one of the Chicago musicians became famous. And that was Lionel Hampton. That's the boy I remember walking around Chicago.
Okay, it's going if you want to state your name.
My name is Preston Jackson. I was born in New Orleans, Louisiana, 1904, January the 3rd. I was born in a part of New Orleans called Carrollton.
Remember just the street and the number?

My mother said Cherokee and Ann, but I don't remember the number just now. I attended pay school, what they called pay school then, before ever going to grammar school. And I started in grammar school at Tom LeFont School.
Was that one of the public schools?
That's a public school.
Was the other a Catholic? What was your religion? Were you Catholic?

Well, no, part of my people, one side a Catholic and the other the Methodist. So I started public school at Tom LeFont School, when I was in 3rd grade. I finished Tom LeFont School and then I, my mother rather, enrolled me in New Orleans University, up at Valmont and St. Charles. Yeah, Bun Johnson went there too, years before.
Yeah.

So I went there for quite a while then we moved to part of New Orleans called the Garden District. And then I later on attended McDonald Number 25. It was down on Rampart Street High School down there. And I left there and went back to New Orleans University.
So when was the first music that you were interested in? Did you start on the trombone or which instrument did you start on?

Well, my first instrument was trombone, but it wasn't my favorite instrument. I'd like to tell you, Bill, about how I come to study the trombone. While talking with Joe Oliver, it must have been somewhere around 1920, 1921, somewhere along there. He, I told Joe Oliver that I was going to take lessons on the trombone. So he says, why don't you try the clarinet? The reason Joe suggested to me to take the, take up the clarinet was because I used to whistle so good. And he said people did. So he thought if a fella could whistle like that, he should take up an instrument where he could maneuver, be more nobility. And so before I could make up my mind just what instrument, I came home one evening and in a little green bag, and after seeing the little green bag I became suspicious of it. I went over to bed and I shook a little, a rattle, and in this little green bag when I opened it was a little Carl Fisher trombone. So my mother just about, she's wanted me to play music and she just about made my mind what instrument I should play. Was it a surprise for Christmas or something? Well no it wasn't a Christmas present. It was about in August. Somewhere around 1920 or 21 something like that. So my first teacher was a fella that called Robinson. I think he had a lot to do with my mother buying the trombone. In fact, I learned later that he purchased the trombone from my mother. He was a trombonist. Was that Zoo? No it wasn't Zoo Robinson. This fella's name was William Robinson. He's from here in Chicago. Oh. Yeah, I think he's a Chicagoan. So I'd taken lessons from him about six months or something like that. And nine months I was playing fair for the length of time that I had the trombone and then I went down to Quinn, I was invited down to Quinn Chapel. There was a lady down there who had a little church band, an orchestra. I don't remember my name now. So I stayed around there about four or five months. Was that in Chicago? That was in Chicago. Chicago, yeah. Then I met Simeon boys. Oh yeah. Al Simeon and Omar Simeon and Bernie Young, Snaggs Jones. Met Bernie Young one day. Bernie and I was in the same town, New Orleans, the same neighborhood. Had been knowing Bernie ever since I was big enough to know a man from a bar. And so I didn't know at that time that Bernie was standing a trumpet out of a corner. He had one before he ever came to New Orleans. I saw him in New Orleans with one. But I had forgotten all about that. So we talked things over and he decided he'd get a band together, which he did. So he got Snaggs and Jones who we went to school with in Tarly Farm. Bernie and I went to Tarly Farm school along with Snaggs. Well the Simeon boys they were from New Orleans but they came from down what they called the French part of town. And the fellas who later became the Simeon boys' brother-in-law by the name of Warden played piano. So Bernie got these fellas together and we formed a little band. Then Snaggs left the band and we got Jimmy McEnry on drums. So we played around in the little bands and we weren't in the union at that time and a fella by the name of Monroe was a big fella, about 250 pounds, was the business agent. He just runnin' from one job to another. In fact he ran us right straight into the union. So then we began to play dances out in Gary and down in the Harbour and places like that. After getting in the union sometime we'd have three dates out there sometime the weekend. We were always single and it was more like a picnic then. Music was really more fun now then than it was today rather. So we began to naturally be interested in music. We began to hang around the different spots like the old Rural Garden, Lake and Garden. We met Joe Oliver, Freddie Kebitt, Manny Poiré, so I knew those fellas in New Orleans before I left. And by that time they'd come up here. Joe Oliver was playing at the, it was Dublin at the Dreamling and going down to the Peking. Peking opened one o'clock. Frederick Kebitt and Manny Poiré, they had the band over at the old Rural Garden, later on named the Lincoln Garden. Rob Palmer and Sugar Johnny and Lil Hardin, who later became Mrs. Louis Armstrong, were playing at Deluxe. It was a place right across from the Dreamling, diagonally on the second floor. So we began to make those places and Joe was a great fellow for shooting, playing bass, a pool. So we'd meet every day at 34th and State, there was a place there. And Dutre and Joe and Johnny and Baby, in fact the whole band except Lil, would meet there and we'd ask different questions. And I'd be getting different pointers from Dutre. I used to sit, I sat behind Dutre about four or five consecutive years. And I was very fortunate in having fellas like that to teach me here in Royal Palmer. Royal Palmer roomed with us, so that was fine. That was...
You read at your home.

Yeah, read at my home. And you can imagine, I didn't give Roy a chance to turn it on unless I was asking him something. So Dutre, he was kind of sickly. And he would let me play for him. He'd go back to Curtain and some kind of medicine in hell, a blend in hell, something like asthma. I learned that he was, while in the Navy he was shutting the hole where the gunpowder was and that caused that. So he'd always say to me, he called me Pardner. He'd say Pardner if I had the good lungs that you have in the wind I sure would be glad. He'd say gee but you have nice lungs. I used to play so loud I guess that's why he spoke about my lungs so I was only too glad to sit down in Joe Oliver's band. So later on Joe Oliver got Joy Field to play trombone, and in the meantime I left Chicago and went to Milwaukee, Wisconsin to join Eli Rice band. I stayed with this band for 14 months and I practiced very diligently. We traveled in Wisconsin, Minnesota, and Michigan for 14 months. Eli Rice was a great singer. His son Sylvester was the drummer, Sylvester Rice. So while up there I began to improve, I began to get a little write-ups like in Marquette, Michigan and different places. And I kept in touch with Joe Oliver and I sent him the write-ups. So Johnny Dodds told me one day after I came back, he said, I told Joe you'd make a good trombone player, I said Joe said you never would make a good trombone player. Well I didn't feel insulted because I respected those fellas. And so while I was with Eli Rice band, after 14 months I came back and I joined Weatherford's band. Weatherford was a great pianist. I think he died in Japan or somewhere. I think India. Yeah, India, somewhere. So I played with him at the old Dreamland, about six weeks and ended up not getting my money for the last week. That's all in the game I guess. If I could collect the money that I have in Gary and Milwaukee and different places, I could probably buy me a nice car or something.
They did cheat the musicians. Yes, yes, yes.
I lost, I have money spread all over the country.
They had a union then but it wasn't able to.

Yeah, well the union wasn't as strong as it is now and the president wasn't the president we have now. I think Harry Gray is one of the greatest presidents we've had. I may be a little prejudiced because I served as a board of director of Local 20 years, and three years on the trial board. This was 23 consecutive years. Are you still official? No, I was defeated. I was defeated there in December. So getting back to this band, Weatherford, it lasted a little while, about four to six weeks, closed up on a Sunday night. Monday night was paid even, came Monday the place was padlocked. I understand this Dr. Johnson padlocked the place on account of rent. I cannot prove that but I heard that. So later on Joe, I advanced so, Joe figured I advanced and was ready for the big time. Snags, by that time Snags was playing drums and George Field on trombone and he had Busta Bailey and on the, Bonnie Bigard and, let's see, Albert Nicholson. Albert Nicholson and Bonnie Bigard. And the bass player was Jackson, the fellow played the bass tuba. He didn't have the string bass.
Remember his first name?

I cannot recall his first name just now, maybe before this interview was over. We can come back to it. But I know him very, Charlie Jackson. Charlie Jackson, he was killed some years later. And I joined Joe Oliver and went to play one in Gaydon with him in South Bend, Indiana, and nothing happened there. I don't remember whether it was the weather or anyhow it was called off when they got to South Bend. So I never did play in Joe Oliver's band. In the meantime the band splits up and John O'Dowd is taking the band over at the place over at the-
Kelly Stables?
Kelly Stables.
Yeah, Kelly Stables.

Yeah, Kelly Stables. And Joe Oliver, he went in with Dave Payton at the plantation. So I visited first one place or another, and Louis Armstrong, by that time Louis left the band and went to New York to join Fletcher Henderson I think. And then Louis goes and joins Fletcher Henderson. And then Ori comes up to join Joe Oliver and he had Bob Schaffner and Tick Gray on trumpets. And he had the same Charlie Jackson on bass, bass horn, and he had Albert Nichols and Bonnie Bigard on the- and Darnell Howard. Well Darnell Howard leaves the band and goes to China a little while after that. In the meantime places began to spring up. Overnight Jimmy Noon was at the nest, right in the next block, the plantation on the corner, diagonally from the sunset. Then the sunset was right across the street. And he had the band. Well this fella came from Ohio and had the band Sammy- Stewart, or something like Sammy Stewart. The bass opened up with Art Sim's band. A fella by the name of Rifferson. The same Fox had the Grand Terrace. They were proprietors. This was Sammy Stewart, or I forget anyhow. I don't think of it before this interview, I'll try it.
That's all right.
If you don't, it's all right. So the musicians just had a ball, especially as young musicians. We had so many places to go. The entertainers was open. We had Wic- Memories are awful bad now.
See, Wycliffe?
Wycliffe, Wycliffe.
It was a company, wasn't it? John Wycliffe.

Yeah, John Wycliffe had the band entertainers. And the Deluxe and the Dreamin' was open. Then you had Jimmy Loom and the Vendome was going big. And Louie was doubling. Later on, before Louie came back, then he doubled from the Vendome. The Vendome to the Sunset. That's when Natty Dominic was playing there with him, you understand? And Dutre. All those bands split up and the men just went like the Four Wings. Dutre was over there with Carol Dixon's band. So I may be in some instances, I may be a little ahead of myself, but I try to rectify
it as I go along.

But I think I was very fortunate in being around during this time, and I think I was very fortunate during this time, and even before that. In New Orleans I remember Joe Oliver. I was going to ask a bit more.
Yeah. If you can go back to your earliest memories, the very first music you ever heard.

Well the very first music I ever heard, we'll deviate a little bit and go back to New Orleans. See I'm a little ahead of myself. The very first one was, I'm very fortunate all the way around Bill, because I lived on Palmer's Avenue and I knew Roy Palmer when he was playing the bass fiddle. I must have been before five years old. And we lived right across the street from one another when I was nothing but a kid. From Roy Palmer.
He really followed you around. He played for my mother during that time.

You see how far I was ahead of my story. He played for my mother on Palmer's Avenue for the fish fries. He was playing the Heller Mandolin and he played bass fiddle then. You see Roy is a musician of many instruments.
Yeah, I know he teaches all that.

And I saw Roy a little later in the arms playing the baritone, I think in the Arnold band. So these things just begin to, you'll have to pardon me because it just began to come to me. That was Sammy Stewart's band was at the old Sunset. You said Stewart. Now that's come to me now. And so we were renting from some people to call their liveazos. And the B-sants was right across the street. They were becoming great ball players, champion B-sants. So I'll go on back to the music now. So there was Nene Bryant, the drummer, and James Williams, he was tabbed for a great. And he left New York with the California League. He died out there. He was tabbed for to be a great clarinet player, I mean right in the same category as Tio and the rest of them. He was young because I saw him. And while attending Tomlin Foreign School every year.
Excuse me for interrupting you again, but about your home and all, did your mother ever sing? Or did anyone? I'm sorry. Well yes, my mother. You don't have to keep those in, it'll pick up anything.

Yeah, my mother was very nice songstress in the church choir, that's where I was told that. But she stopped singing when I was somewhere around two or three years old. She had trouble with her throat.
You probably remember hearing her sing earlier when you were a baby.
Yeah, but I'd be here singing at home, but my mother had a nice voice.
And so- Any other relatives play any music?

I don't remember any relatives of mine that ever played any music. And as I know of, I had an uncle supposed to graduate this conservatory in Boston, a great uncle but I never did see him, my mother told him about it but I never did see it. And Celestan, the great Celestan, that was coming to him every year in June when school closed, they'd hire Celestan's band to play for us. That's when I first saw Henry Zeno. And Celestan, and Johnny Dodson, fellas like that. So we would get around those fellas and the next day we'd have a whistling contest between me and Snagg Jones and Ovid Farnett and the fellas like that. So when I went back to New Orleans later on with Lil Armstrong they wasn't surprised that I was playing music because Snagg used to get the rounds of the chairs and we'd play, get them high box steps like they had in New Orleans and we'd whistle and have to do it, sometimes trills. And of course Snagg he started playing drums before me. He played with this fellow, this fiddle player in New Orleans, not Robichaud. He played with the show.
Piron?

Piron. He played with Piron, the fellas, see, long before I thought about playing. But we went to school together in the third and fourth grade. Then there was Humphrey, Willie Humphrey, Willie Humphrey. The reason I'm breaking up some of these fellas, Bill, while reading the book that you gave me, I noted in there, I think it was Dominic who said that the musicians downtown read and
the musicians in downtown didn't read.
I begged to differ with him. I'm going a little further back now, Bill, let's begin to come to me. Professor George Correa was a neighbor of mine.
George? George Correa.
Now I read something about George Correa in some other books about a year ago, another book that had been edited. And there was Professor Humphrey.
Surely he read music.
George Correa.
Yeah, sure, I know. And Roy did. And Roy did.

Roy read music. And so I don't see where they got the idea that Uptown the fellas didn't. Maybe Dominic was a little, we're good friends, but maybe a little precious because Dominic was from downtown, you see.
Well, I don't think Dominic, some other people told us that, like some people said that Bolden didn't read. Well maybe Bolden didn't.
There's a whole lot of them white musicians didn't read either.
George Brunus. Yeah.

See what I'm talking about? So I mean I lived right across the street from Professor George Correa, and when I lived on Upper Line Street I was only two blocks from the Humphreys, and Mrs. Humphrey, old man Humphrey's daughter, taught me in the fourth grade at Tarly Farm School. And she taught us a little music there. And so she knew music and evidently I think she must have gotten from her father. And Willie Humphrey today, if he's still living, he reads a lot of music. His brother Earl was a trombone player, then he has a younger brother, plays the drum, Pricy.
Well he's in the Eureka, the trumpet player, and he's the leader of the Eureka band, the brass band.

Well all right then. So they cannot tell me that the musicians didn't read because I begged to differ with them. Because when I went to New Orleans in 21 to visit, I brought some music down there and I did a little playing around there with Red A. Well Red A didn't do any of the French, or Morris French didn't read either. But some of the men, like Zip, some of the men didn't read because I passed out the parts. And they did read. But Red A had a good ear once they played something over. Well once or twice and they had it. So I used to sit in with those fellas at San Suzy Hall in 1921. I was just playing a fair myself at the time. But Morris French was supposed to be one of the top trombone players during that time. He was with Red A's band, see? And so I know that some of the music, it didn't make any difference what part of New Orleans the fella did.
No I don't think so either.

And Celestan, Celestan has always read music. Guy Kelly made read music. I know so many fellas that read music. He can't tell me that they didn't read music. And so as I was foreseeing about Celestan, that was a band I really enjoyed. The drums, the drummer, Henry Zeno, used to take a solo, or maybe about 24 bars. That's the tune that was playing. And then the drums, and then the drums, and then it falls in again.
You understand? They take the drum solo in those days then.

Yeah. And then I began to get a little larger and a little older naturally, and I go a little straight a little farther from home. And I began to see Red Happy. Now Red Happy, I'll tell you, was the greatest drummer as far as execution.
Well Lee Collins always said that.

Yeah, that ever hitting New Orleans as far as execution. I read Happy would have a lot of things to back him, over him, and everywhere, you know. And he'd make a break and hit all those different things, and coming on time he was a great drummer. I think he was even greater than Baby Dotson. Baby Bots was a good drummer, was a fine drummer, as in his prime he was still a good drummer. But Happy was supposed to have been the best. And the old man, and his first band in 1911, Cottrell. Oh yeah, the old man. Yeah, Cottrell and Zeno. Zeno and now here's Tubby Hall and Minor Hall. A relative of theirs taught me at New Orleans University. I remember seeing Tubby Hall when I was a little fellow, I only lived, they lived around Cadie Street, right by the La Rocca Boys. The La Rocca Boys, people, had a grocery store on Ferret. It was either Cadie and Ferret or Jen and Ferret. I knew that. Now those boys come on that first, what do you call them? Original Dixieland band.
Yeah, original Dixieland band.

That's where the La Rocca Boys come from. So Tubby Hall and his brother, Minor, I saw them playing drums when I was a kid, you understand? And they are cousins to the Humphreys. Yeah, they are cousins to the Humphreys. Yeah, so I saw Happy, then I began to see Mud Carey, Jack Carey, two brothers. Then I began to attend the dances. I'd sneak away from home and borrow somebody's pants, long pants, you know, and sometimes we'd have to saw them down to my side one way or the other, and I'd go to these dances unbeknown to my mother. She didn't know I was attending dance until the lady crossed the street. Saw me one night and told her. Then I began to see fellas, like the whole Kid Orr's band, Vigionny Dots, Orr and Mud Carey on the trumpet, Henry Zeno and fellas.
Where did you hear those? At the dances?

I saw them up there, yeah, I heard them at the ballpark, Third and Willa. And they used to have dances there. And I'd hear them at Third and Willa, Six and Willa, wherever there was a saloon. Well you'd hear that music for miles and as kids we'd just start the looping and follow the sound. That was National Park, yeah, Third and Willa, National Park. Punch totals.
Yeah.

That's where I'd hear them. And so there was Tick Chambers, Kohl's, Lawn Parties on Josephine Street. Tick was playing there, you see? So I mean it just was one of those things where you had to hear that music. And on every Monday or Sunday there was advertisement, here comes a horse and wagon, I guess that's where that tailgate come, because the trombone player was always on the end, because he needed room for his slide. So that's why I said I'm very fortunate to have been born in New Orleans and I'm grateful because as a lover of music I came right from the ground floor. I didn't have to go anywhere to hear it, my neighbors was musicians, like the Careers, the Humphreys, and all those people was musicians. But I never studied any music at that time, I just-
How do you spell that name, the Careers, do you remember?
I see, I think it's C-E-R-E-R.
Because there's French names-
Yeah, C-E-R-E-R-E-R. Yeah, thanks. Something like that. I think it was George Careers.
Yeah, we can look it up in the book.
He was a professor of Careers, yeah. And he had a brother called Sidney that played the tenor saxophone. So before I left New Orleans-
Well when did you leave about?

In 1917. I arrived in Chicago January the 3rd, 1917. I was thirteen years old. And it wasn't long before I began to hear them talking about Louis Armstrong. My, at the time it was Joe Oliver. I'd seen them fellas bucking one another, him and Mutt. René, I hadn't heard of René. And I hadn't heard of Louis because I saw Louis. And while attending the tomlaphone school there was a lot there, it had holes in it as much as three and four feet deep and they filled it in and whatever they could and they made a playground of it, which they still had the tomlaphone playground. And Louis was back at the Jones home at the time. So they had the band to come out to dedicate, they was dedicating the tomlaphone playground. I remember the truant officer very well too, this was Mrs. Boyd, yeah, she used to run us all the time, Mrs. Boyd. And I saw Louis play the trumpet and he played so well, he was so cocky, you know, he stood out front to where they all spoke about it. And that was just about 50 feet from Bernie Young's house. I mean he lived right kind of diagonally from the playground. And so when I laid on, after some of the boys came up here, they weren't musicians but they were talking about Louis Armstrong, I said he has to blow something if he can out-blow Joe out of him. I said, or Mud, either one. They said, oh man, we got Buddy P.T. and Randy A2. He said, they always bucking one another. I said, man, you ought to see what's going on there all now. I said, Louis Armstrong is the best. He said, that man can really play. So I said, I don't believe he can out-blow Joe out of him. So here's where I was fussing again. Later on Joe out of him comes up in late 1918 I think. Then later on about 21, Louis Johnson. I'm sitting on the stand when Louis walks in there with a brown suit on with one of these sailors and tan shoes on a Sunday night when he first came in. Later on I played, the little band we had together, we played at the reception for Lil and Louis at the wedding reception. And Louis told me then, he says, if I ever have a band, you keep on studying, if I ever have a band of my own, you're going to be my trombone player. And true enough, Louis after he came back from New York, I was the first fellow that looked up and to join his band. I was with him about 14 months and I never will forget that Bill. I never will forget that.
That's the end of this.
I was talking about Oliver all day. Joe Oliver was a good pool player as I told you.
Oh yeah, he used to play with him.
You're a good pool player too.
You can catch him by one o'clock every day.
Well there's a fella Giannis Censier, you run into Giannis Censier?
Oh yes, I've known him. He's a nice fella.
Yeah, he was with that hot five.
He's in California now. Oh he's in California now.

Yeah, he's a plaster or something. Yeah, I saw him last time I was in y'all, he was making plenty of money. He was doing a whole lot of building there. Now Giannis Censier, he came up later on. Now when these two boys, Albert, this big guard, now they call him Bonnie, you know they call him Bonnie, see? And Albert, Albert, that's Albert in French, you understand? And so I saw them there, Rudy Richards was the other saxophone player with Joe Oliver at the Lincoln Garden. I was at the Lincoln Garden the night that the place caught fire. Oh really? Yeah. A fella flew around there to match and set the place on fire. That's what happened. I was supposed to join Joe Oliver. That's why I didn't join him, because the place caught on fire. Mrs. Majors was the proprietor. They had a fella by the name of Bud Redd, who was the manager. And old King Jones, the fella who used to spiel in front of the survive when they had the
fights, he was the instructor back there.

Yeah, well he was a regular fashion player. Twenty-five or thirty suits of clothes. They'd give him suits of clothes just to advertise. I heard he died not so long ago in New York. And getting back to, well Lee played with Joe Oliver at the Lincoln Garden too, see? Well now the Sidewalk Blues, Lee wrote the Sidewalk Blues and Jellie Roten, turned it over to Jellie Roten and Jellie Roten had it to copyright it. And that was the last, that was the last, maybe Lee told you about it.
But Lee never did talk about it?

No, well that's what happened. Well Lee was playing there, he was playing there with Rudy and Nichols and his boys, they were playing together there. And then Joe was on the drums. And Joe lived right there at 31st Estate. Joe was teaching this boy, this Italian boy, I call his name. Penico? Yeah, he was teaching Penico. Yeah, he was teaching Penico. And Joe, he'd be taking a whole lot of time up with them young musicians, time with him, I mean as far as teaching them and telling them this and telling them that and telling them this. Now Joe, what broke up there, what caused the downfall of Joe Oliver's band was Joe had a contract to record for Jeanette. And Joe decided to do some recording for Victor or one of those others. And what they told Joe says, well anybody can tell that's your band, says any way that you could make some substitution so that it would sound a bit different. So Joe didn't want to get in trouble with Jeanette either, so he substituted, asking for Dutre and noon for Johnny Dodds. That caused the trouble. Well they didn't find out immediately. It may have been two or three when the records were released. Then they heard the records and that's when the trouble comes. So Johnny pulls away from Joe and goes over down Rush Street. I played there once with him. And Joe gets Bob Shottley, Tick Gray, the fellas, and goes in the plantation. He plays at the Lincoln Garden or Royal Garden, they change the name you know once or twice.
Oh Tick Gray, is that any relation to the union president?
No, no relation at all. Is he from Chicago or New Orleans?
Yeah, Chicago.

And Bob Shottley, he's from St. Louis, he played with Charlie Creston. He's playing now. Yeah, yeah. Well that's about the same Bob Shottley. So he gets that band and Ori on the trombone and they play the plantation. Well Johnny and Dutre is playing with Dominic. Dominic's playing trumpet on down Rush with Baby Dodds. So that caused the split in the band. So Joe, after there, he leaves the plantation. In the meantime, Louie's in New York, Joe goes to New York and forms a band. He fooled around the Middle West a while with Red Allen playing with him and over there. They came and played against us with Bunny Young's band at the Wisconsin Roof. But there wasn't no match for us because they wasn't together. They were a band five years ago with three good arrangements and most of the bands stood at the Marquette University branch. You see I was studying myself to do harmony in theory myself. And we were on the job every night. Now maybe the old Joe Alva band would have given us fits, but not that Joe Alva band except for Henry Allen. And so there was some talk about him trying to get the job but it just blew him out of there. We had Randolph there, it wasn't Randolph. You know that boy played a whole lot of horn. If he was from St. Louis, where are we from? That boy, and it just blew him out of there. And Joe, Joe was beginning to have him in trouble with his teeth anyhow. And so we just blew him on, there was nothing. There was a whole lot of bands that had been up there that was better than that, we just blew him out of there. And so then Joe goes on out east and he flew around out there. Well the next time I saw Joe I stand by this hotel over there at South Park in the Ritz. By the Ritz. And he came through there and he lost quite a bit of weight. Then I meet him, when I'm with Louis Armstrong, I meet him down in Galveston. He still had a band. Well I guess you read about the trouble he had about the buses. Well he was having his telephone. He was on his way out. He was on his way out then. Yeah. He was on his way out then. But he was telling me, he heard us tell me, he says, boy you sure did come along on the trombone. You sure did come along on the trombone. He says, I didn't think he'd ever make it. I stumbled around a long time Bill, but things had just begun to come to me. The first thing, I didn't want to play the trombone. See I wanted to like, I was, he said, whew, whew, whew, whew, whew, whew. I can't whistle and say it like I used to. But I could whistle, I could go, whew, whew, whew, whew, whew, whew, whew, whew, whew, you know, things like that.
Well I wanted to play the clarinet.

Did you ever get the clarinet at all? That's why it'd take me so long with the trombone, see. No, never did, nothing but the trombone. After I began to play it and people would take notes and I'd say well I'd just go ahead on through with it. I'm glad I did now. Because they told me, he says, there isn't but a few, at that time you didn't have the musicians they have now, everywhere you look, he says there ain't but a few good trombone players around here. And I held the top up top there around here, not bragging, for years around here. And just like Roy told me, he says, you learn that trombone if you learn it right, he says, you'll hold your line. And at one time there was Blake, Al Wynn, myself, and this boy would die. Billy, he was a singer too, he died. There was about four of us, and Taylor, there was about four or five. Blake was a good one, Al was good, and this boy Taylor was good, he played with O. Hines when he was at the old Grand Territory. He's dead now too. Yeah. And it came in and the advice he gave to me when I sat down in the pit and played them overtures and things. Well now, here's another man, I must attribute my success, what success I had, Art Stewart, the big K.P. band, morning, noon, and night and things like that. He always hollering at me, get in there! All right, I go to New York with a brass band, about eighty pieces. I don't know how to walk and step. I attribute that to them fellas hollering at me, get in the step there, rookie, get in the step there. We went to New York in the 20s there, but it must have been a hundred and some pieces, Bob Shaffin, the best cream of Chicago. And we walked from Harlem to Central Park. We taught New York Open. We played a concert in a little town out of New York. We camped right on Boston Road out there. Oh I could just talk for years but I just jumped from one place to another. Now Joe had a nice wife and a daughter named Ruby. I visited Joe's house so many times I just can't count. I ate that gumbo and whatnot. He had a cruel wife. Somebody said he was a big eater, is that right? Oh my goodness, red beans and rice. Now that's Louis Armstrong when they had the band Savoy. They had them parties and red beans and rice. They go to some lady's house there on South Park and she's cooking the red beans and rice, and that's when they had Clarence Black's band and Louis's band, later on they had it. Now that's a man, Charlie Elder.
I talked to him the other day.

He had a studio right there at 36th Estate you know. He had the band in Milwaukee, the Wisconsin roof, before Sims had it. He comes or he leaves there and goes to Savoy. That's when Sims goes on in there and when Sims is about a year or so I go in there with Sims. But he had a good band, he had a good band, he had good Harmon's Bremen. He had Riverview. He and Cook, those fellas, they had some of the best jobs to be had. McGuire's down on Clark Street. I follow Roy and Dutray and him all around. And I get into places like McGuire's and all those places. See? I get into those places. But I follow Dutray. It was an honor to carry them fellas' horns. I carried the horns for them. And I don't regret it. I ever met the Lil' Whitties was great. And I see them meet them fellas and we had a little band, we copied right behind Joy of them, note for note. Every time they made a record, note for note, note for note. But he was playing this Snaggit, that Snaggit and all that stuff, note for note. And we recorded. I have a record here now I think of Buddy Helms' band. One side is Joff and the other is Buddy Helms. On the Paramount. We recorded. We recorded the Tin Roof Band. Did you ever have any record? Yeah, I have that record. And then I had a little band of my own with all this stuff. Did you ever hear that record? I found the- Yeah. I recorded my own little band of Shirley Clay. That's nice. Shirley Clay, you hear? Yeah. That was nice. Later on they played with Don Redmond, Shirley Clay, nice trumpet player. I mean they had a lot of good trumpet players from St. Louis and Kansas City. I mean all of them didn't come from New Orleans, see? But they were the pioneers, you see, and a lot of those boys went on that boat down there, they're sitting in this boat down there in New Orleans, and got a lot of stuff from them boys, that's possible. But I know like Bob Schaffner, Bob Schaffner's a good Dixieland, you've heard him over there, and Bob Schaffner and this boy had St. Louis all locked up, Charlie- Crep. Charlie Crep, yeah. He was great. He was great too. You see what I'm talking about? Yeah, sure. And they had musicians from out east that was good too. But Chicago was the king, New York at that time, the great Fletcher Henderson and the Duke of Henderson wasn't heard of. Wasn't heard of. They wasn't heard of. They wasn't heard of. When Joe Oliver had his band, that great band of his, they wasn't heard of. Fletcher later on, St. Louis and Tommy Ladner, that's another boy. That Tommy Ladner could play a whole lot of trumpet. He joined Fletcher later on. See what I'm talking about? He said for those fellas, Fletcher didn't have the band. Those fellas helped make the band that Fletcher laid on. Hawkins, I just heard a little bit about Hawkins. Then we had Stumpy Evans. You ever hear of Stumpy Evans?
Yeah, he's from Denver but he's been there.

His home was in Texas, but I lived in there. But lung trouble I think he died. But that boy was wonderful. He used to tell me, you should hear Coleman Hawkins. Now that must have been in 1923. You should hear Coleman Hawkins.
You should hear Coleman Hawkins. Yeah.

So Joe Oliver, now there's the whole, there's Bix Bydebeck, Tea Garden. I saw Bix Bydebeck. See I have some, I saw something where a whole lot of people didn't see it. And I'm great. Bix Bydebeck was a great trumpet player. They had a whole lot of great white musicians too. There was this boy, this client, this player, what was his name, from around Chicago here? Tex. Yeah, Tex was great. Now that was Art Castle. I played against Art Castle with Dennis Goodman out the midway. And Moksi was the trumpet player. Moksi. See, great. See what I'm talking about? At the sunset you could see Tea Garden, once in a while Mip Moe would be in town, Bix Bydebeck, Tish, Art Castle, they'd all be there in their tuxedas. They'd reserve a whole table. At the old Royal Garden and the sunset, they'd be there. Tea Garden, all those fellas would be there. Right there, listening to them fellas. I got a chance to see all them fellas. I didn't know who they were. There was no introduction or nothing like that. But later on seeing the pictures, I found out who they were. I heard Tea Garden, I always did love Tea Garden playing. Always did. And I'd like to know who they were, I'd ask who, that's Jack Tea Garden. I finally met Tea Garden. And I'm glad to meet Tea Garden, because Tea Garden up to the day plays great trombone. Now Jimmy Harrison, I never saw him but I heard him. He died when he was in the yard with Louis. He was great. He was the king at the time. He was really the king at the time, Jimmy Harrison. And then here comes Mip Moe. Now Mip Moe was playing before I ever played. Mip Moe and Red, not Red Nickles, it's Pennies, who was that? Yeah, Pennies, yeah. That was a nice bunch wasn't it? Yeah. That was a good bunch wasn't it?

I was going to ask you, I don't want to put you on the spot, but I mean if you don't mind saying who would be your favorite trombone player. There's nothing wrong with having a favorite, I mean that's not insulting the other people, because I know you like a lot of them, you told me you liked a whole bunch of them. Well if you had to pick one or two.

Well if I had to pick a trombone player, these modern day trombone players, I'd have to pick them from the style. Now for that bebop, I like some of it, some of it I don't. But for the bebop, there's K. Wenge and there's J.J. Johnson, there's two best. I mean of the old times, your whole life, it's the best you ever heard.
The best I ever heard.

Oh you're just talking about the old music, or the old music, or just everybody. Just everybody in the world. Well that's kind of hard because we had a boy that called Big Green. And for playing blues, according to what kind of music played, for playing blues, Big Green, and I love Vic, and it's just, it's kind of hard. The old time. And that was Roy, I'd put Roy against any of them. And that was Jimmy Harrison, I heard him but I never saw him. I didn't hear much of him though. But going from what Lou and them boys say, and the look that I heard of him, it's kind of hard. And there's T. Gordon, he plays so much trombone player, so much trombone, a wonderful trombone player, I'd be afraid to say I was too good. I don't know, I was, just like I said, this boy for execution, this bebop, this J.J. and this K. Windy, for that style, it was the best I ever heard. I never heard fellas get off. I think they're playing valves though. Must be. Yeah, they must be, for that execution. See I never saw them just in person playing. So I don't know whether they're playing valves or the slide. So but I'd pick, for the old musician, the old New Orleans musician, I'd pick Roy Palmer. I'd take Roy Palmer. Maybe I'm a bit prejudiced. I'd pick him over Detroit. Dutrae taught me too. But Dutrae didn't play as much as he did. Now O'Reay played a whole lot too, but not as much as Roy Palmer. He didn't seem to care much about Roy Palmer.
I wonder why. Well he never made a lot of records.
No, he didn't seem to care much about that.
Maybe it was the way Roy Carriott still. I just had to be a football player. Maybe he had the reputation of going to sleep on a job or something, you know?
Yeah, and I just felt like Dickie Wells, he was a wonderful trombone player. He still plays.

I was going to ask again, before I forget it, about Joe Oliver again. Was he really a good pool player? Did he play all the time? Who was that? Joe Oliver. Oh yeah, he was good. You know he had one bad eye.

And he's good, a good pool player. Yeah. He had one bad idea. He had one bad idea. He had one bad idea. He had one bad idea. He had one bad idea. He had one bad idea. He had one bad idea. He had one bad idea. He had one bad idea. He had one bad idea. He had one bad idea. He had one bad idea. He had one bad idea. He had one bad idea. He had one bad idea. He had one bad idea. He had one bad idea. He had one bad idea. He had one bad idea. He had one bad idea. He had one bad idea. He had one bad idea. He had one bad idea. Now you take Armani for the type of music that he played, he was all right. But I wouldn't put him in the same category as Earl Hines. And there's Teddy Wilson. Now there's Kate Johnson, another trombone player where he's playing, Bud Johnson's brother. He was wonderful I think too. After immediately he was Armstrong, he joined Armstrong. And he played some wonderful solos, breaks and things. So I mean there's so many. And there's Vic. Vic got a style all his own. That's Lawrence Brown. I mean there's so many. And nowadays they're jumping up. These youngsters are playing, they seem to have so much more execution.

I was going to ask you again to change the subject. We'll finish up in a few minutes now. About some of the New Orleans places like Miss Cole's Lawn Parties. Did you ever go there or were you just a kid?

I just peeped at them. They wouldn't allow me in there. They wouldn't allow me in there. I just peeped at them. But I did go to the National Park and dance by Joe's music before I was acquainted with Joe.
What was that?
Was it the- Then we had that old second line too. You heard about the second line.
I want to ask about the phrase, let's talk a minute about the National Park. Was that for dances or did they play for ball?
That was a baseball park.
Did they play for baseball games too? They put a platform down.
No they might advertise a baseball game. Very seldom there.
Would that be at night time or day time? The baseball game? No I mean when Joe would play there.

Oh that'd be at night time. At night time. Record or dance then? Yeah. They'd put all the lights out and play just about midnight. All the lights out and then they'd start playing the blues. Well I lived about a mile from there and I used to sit down and hear Joe this is clear. The music was right there. The outside sound. Better than the inside. And I was hearing Louis play before I ever knew it was Louis Armstrong. I didn't know it. Just like I told you I saw Louis when he first was playing. But I made a trip back down there and I heard him, I didn't know it was Louis, I wondered who he was. I was down there for a few days, I'd forgotten. Then the boys began to tell me about Louis. Some friends of mine began to tell me about Louis. Now Louis, when, he's a man like this, I'm going to tell you about Louis, I can't praise him too much. Louis put me in the band and he kept me in the band. I didn't have so many friends in that band, for different reasons. Maybe because I never cared for liquor, or maybe other reasons. I'd stick in bed and I got out of bed in New Orleans there, I stayed at the Page Hotel. The Page Hotel?
Yeah.

They turned that down at last. Yeah. Mike comes and tells me that I'm fired. I go over to Patterson Hotel, where Louis was, and they asked him what's the matter, Louis. I said, she'll give me a notice if I'm fired. I just stick in bed and I had a lumbago. Louis says, I put you in the band and you're going to stay in this band, I don't care what Collins said. And he and Collins had a big fuss. So I love Louis. You understand? I love Louis. I mean the reputation of being with Louis Armstrong. He lives today. People say he put me there. He used to be Louis Armstrong. I mean it's a certain lot of prestige. The last time I saw Louis here, he said, what was the same album? He said those records we made when I was with it are great. He said I played great. But I think some records I made since then, that I played better. But I've never been able to play on the records, when I just play I live my heart, because I always tighten up to a certain degree. I've never been free. You know, I never felt free. I don't know whether I was afraid of making the mistakes. Now I made some records with the Half Pint Jackson, they had them in England, and it was raving about the solo I played on it. But I don't have none of the records. I'd be so glad if I had the records. You see I didn't buy the records as these record collectors did. I threw them and every time I move or break some of them, they had to go by. I stumbled upon one of Joe Oliver's records about three years ago in the alley. And I looked at it and I saw Jeanette there and I died for it. I whispered to them and said, well you crazy? I said, don't you see this is Joe Oliver's record. I bet half of it. Oh just half of it. Half of it. Now I kept it and finally lost, you see what I'm talking about? Just half of the record. So I've got a record here now.
Maybe I can find that 15 cents for you someday.
I sure would.
Now here's an old term, huh?
The Southern Storm and the Devil Street Blues. See that?
That's the one, the Young's Creole.
Yeah, the Young's Creole. That's the first little band I played in.
The first little band I played in. So I was going to ask a little bit to you about the parades and the second line.

Yeah, well the second line, the second line. I guess I just always was crazy about music. Doing that whistling and going on I did. I guess it just was destined for me to be a musician. I believe in predestination. I believe when a person is first born, that is like a big book, there's so much he's supposed to accomplish in life, you understand? And then leave this world. Now the way I used to whistle and take the sticks and pound and go on like that, and hear that music, I could follow the music for miles. It's a funny thing about music, I guess that's why they have these bands in the Army. You can march miles by music and you don't get tired. You see what I'm talking about? Now I'd march all the way down to the Seven Ward, from the 12th Ward to the Seven Ward, and the only reason I'd come back with the boys was to run me back. You had to fight when you'd go down in the Seven Ward, see? Or the Third Ward was supposed to be one of the worst in New Orleans. They called that the battlefield. See? That's where Lewis from the Third Ward was. They called that the battlefield, around Pedilla Street, Gravy Street. Well you know what went on there around Gravy and Pedilla and even Cross Canal Street, you read about it. The red light and everything, see? Well next to the, around Iberville and Vien, well we used to sneak in there and be run out, you know what they had there. Well when you come around Gravy Street, around Saratoga, Liberty and all around there, that's the parish prison there, that prison there, see it's torn down now, they don't have any more of that. So they all were. Well it was rough and tough around there. But when we hit around there, somebody would walk up and sock us and start us on the way, maybe it'd be six or seven of us, or maybe it'd be twenty of those. But them fellas would play that Diddy Ramble. Diddy Ramble.
Oh Diddy Ramble. Oh diddy Ramble. Oh diddy Ramble around the town. To the little butchie cut him down.

Oh diddy Ramble. Well you guys would be coming along, diddy Ramble, and they're wibble and they're wibble and bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo You see what I'm talking about? That's called the second line. The second line was outnumbered the procession of the other wives. See what I'm talking about? And so I started doing that and I always did, humming around, I guess my mother could see it. And so I owe a lot to my mother. I stuck with it until she died Bill. I owe a lot to my mother.
So you never regret that.

My mother started to call me playing music. I never would have got one myself, and then she had the little horn on the bed, I never would forget that. And I stuck with it until she passed. And so that's all I could do. But I guess she could see that I wanted to play music. She could see. I used to could whistle, so I'd whistle anything anybody played, and so could Snagg's Joan. And Joe Oliver used to have me to whistle to get ideas from me. Now you might not believe that. So he had me and Snagg's to whistle, and a couple of nights Joe would turn the horn to we even play it. That's what he really would do. That's how good I used to whistle. And so I started from all around, must have been eight or nine years old, I began to run behind them bands.
You could hear them for miles. Did you ever play a little Ken flute or anything?

No, nothing, no Ken or anything. And I didn't, I told my mom, I said I don't want to play this, I said I want to play a clarinet. So she told Mr. Robinson, she says, his name was William Robinson, she said he don't want to play the trombone, he wants the clarinet. And so he told me, he says, listen, a good trombone player can always find work. Well it's just the reverse now. Was that in Chicago or New Orleans when you got here on? That was in Chicago. I didn't even touch yesterday on New Orleans.
Well did any of the kids when they went on those parades, did they ever play any little Ken flute or anything with the other band in the second line?
The only first time I saw anybody playing a thing like that was Louis Armstrong.
He had one of them, you know the slide. You mean the kids didn't play along with the band in the street or anything?

I never saw any, I never saw any of them. Once I heard that they did. Singling and whistling, you know it was a great whistling time. It's good for singing and whistling. Like all them tunes like Sister Kate by Rack, that's Louis Armstrong's tune. That's the same. I don't want to get in no trouble. No, Louis told me that and Natty Dominick said that he wrote on.
Well I heard that before I ever come down.
That tune I heard it before it came from New Orleans.
Well did you hear any music in the churches much? Your mother, which church did she sing?
Well it was Williams Chapel, that's where I was Christian. I was Christian at Williams Chapel up there, I think it was up on Cherokee Street. Williams Chapel.
Was that Baptist or Methodist?
Methodist. Methodist. Some of them was Catholic and some of them were like the Marchion and the French one.
But you don't remember hearing many spirituals or gospel music in the church you think when

you were up there? I heard them at camp meetings. I threw in one of the same park as a camp meeting, I always remember, yeah. And it's just like I heard Mahalia Jackson last night. I mean that music's got a swing to it. When that piano starts to kind of vamp and then you know give it an intro, it's a swing there. And I've been hearing that all my life. It's a swing there. Now about those Methodists and the Catholics and the Protestants, a boy named Chigar, I was raised up. His name was, I think his name was Initial Jewels. And I used to go to the Catholic Church there on Faurant and Napoleon Avenue. I used to go. I mean that's the only church in the Orange that the both races did in the mixing. I mean I can go way back then. And the Catholics always seemed to be better to color than the other people. Because I went to the church several times, you know, and we sat where we weren't sitting and there wasn't nobody saying anything to him. It's not great a day. But it's probably that way of the day. Now this Chigar and his brother, we called him Tutu, Chigar's name was Initial Jewels, the Creole people. And so, but getting back to the Catholic, now the Elick Marchand, Joe Marchand, my cousin, they were strictly Catholic people. And the Francois was Catholic people. Then the Mauritius, the Methodists. So I was a Christian Methodist. And it's been that way ever since. So at Second Line, every kid of any size, if there's people who are not watching, you join that parade, and you're just marching and marching and you find yourself in another part of town. And when you get in the sides, them gangs, they run you, they get behind you and run you back where you come from. They'd ask you for a nickel or something, if you didn't give it to them they'd hit you or anything like that. They had them gangs they used to fight. But they wasn't like these gangs now, you know, they wasn't the guns and things. These kids now are killing one another. They hit you with your fists or maybe throw bricks at you or something like that. But the first time I saw a lawyer I never will forget. I wish you could have saw him, Bill. He just stood up there in front of the rest of the boys. The Joneses home, baby. Yeah, with a sticker just like this, a picture just like this. If you ever saw the picture, that's the way he was. He was destined to be great, Bill. He was destined to be great. You could see it in and in. And he couldn't have been over about twelve years old at the best. Because he was back there with another boy from the old named Gus. And I know some other boys played with him back there. You ever have George Washington strombone playing with him? Yeah, sure. He played with Buddy T. P.T. and then. Well George and a fellow called Frazier played bass horn. He played back there with Lewis. Gus, George and Frazier, they played back there. And they used to play this Maryland, well that's the tune they play, that's one of the tunes they play, that Tonlefong playground. At the first time I saw Lewis, and I told Lewis about it, I said you know, I saw you, but I didn't know who you was, that's who he was. And we came up here, we made friends, I'll never forget that first night he hit Chicago. And then he and Liv fell in love and we got married.
How was the hat was it, you said he had on a sailor hat or something?
He had on one of these sailors, you know straw hats? Oh, I know. With a brown backsuit. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

I think later his mind even went. Yeah, yeah, he had a brother named Henry Rene. He's still living, but he doesn't play anymore. Yeah, he's a drummer. He's enjoying church now or something. He's either a preacher or something. Anyway, he won't play dance either.

He's a drummer, but Rene, he was a trumpet player. He's one of the best I heard. I mean, he stayed up there in the upper register all the time. And when he was at his best, he'd give Louie, when Louie was at his best, all Louie wanted.
